draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A use the eraser to transfer a substance onto the paper, such as graphite or ink, so that it marked the message?"}
review:
This is a useful next question: it tests whether the eraser left a mark by depositing material, rather than by indenting or changing something already on the page. But the two “no” answers do not establish that A added a substance, and graphite or ink are only examples—not supported facts.

A slightly more discriminating version: **“Did the eraser itself leave a visible mark on the paper?”** If yes, ask what produced it; if no, explore other ways the eraser helped create or reveal the message.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the eraser itself leave a visible mark on the paper?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A use the eraser as a stamp to transfer ink or another marking substance onto the paper?"}
review:
The proposed question is plausible: the “no” to making the message by removing or altering something suggests a substance may have been added. But nothing yet supports the specific “stamp” mechanism, and “yes and no” about a visible mark could mean the mark was only partial or became meaningful later.

A more discriminating question: **“Was the message visible on the paper immediately after A used the eraser?”** That separates direct transfer from a mark that requires a later reveal.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the message visible on the paper immediately after A used the eraser?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A apply ink, paint, or another substance to the eraser and use it as a stamp to print the message?"}
review:
The proposal is plausible, but “no” to the removal-versus-addition question doesn’t establish that A added ink or used the eraser as a stamp. The “yes and no” about a visible mark also leaves unclear whether the eraser transferred material or acted in some other way.

A more discriminating question: **“Did A use the eraser to transfer a marking substance onto the paper?”** If yes, ask next whether it was used as a stamp.

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A use the eraser as a stamp, applying ink or another marking medium from elsewhere to the paper?"}
review:
The proposed stamp question is likely redundant: the prior answer says A did **not** use the eraser to transfer a marking substance, which appears to rule out stamping ink or another medium from elsewhere.

A more discriminating question would be: **“Was the message readable only under a particular angle or lighting condition?”** The current feedback establishes immediate visibility, but not whether visibility depends on how the paper is viewed.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the message readable only under a particular angle or lighting condition?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the paper thermal paper, so that rubbing it with the eraser generated heat that made the message appear?"}
review:
This is a plausible hypothesis, but the clues don’t establish that the paper was thermal or that frictional heat caused the message. It may also conflict with the earlier “no” to making the message by altering something already on the paper: thermal paper would typically change color through a heat-triggered reaction.

A more discriminating question is: **“Did rubbing cause a heat-triggered color change in the paper itself?”** That tests the mechanism without assuming the paper was thermal.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did rubbing the eraser cause the paper itself to change color through heat?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A use the eraser as a stamp, with letters or symbols on it that printed the message onto the paper?"}
review:
The stamp idea is possible, but “printed” usually implies transferring ink, pigment, or residue—apparently ruled out by the “no” to transferring a marking substance. It also assumes the eraser already had letters or symbols on it.

A more discriminating question would be: **“Was the eraser specially shaped or marked with the message before A used it?”**
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the message encoded in the eraser’s shape or surface before A used it?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the eraser trigger a chemical reaction in the paper that made the message appear?"}
review: The chemistry hypothesis is plausible, but nothing in the feedback establishes that a chemical reaction occurred—or that it occurred *in the paper*. A more discriminating question would be: **“Did contact with the eraser make the message visible through a chemical change, rather than a physical or optical effect?”** This tests the mechanism without assuming where the reaction happens.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did contact with the eraser make the message visible through a chemical change, rather than a physical or optical effect?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A use the eraser to make holes, tears, or other permanent physical damage to the paper that formed the message?"}
review:
The question is plausible, but “other permanent physical damage” is broad and overlaps several possible mechanisms. It also doesn’t distinguish obvious damage like holes from subtler abrasion or changes in the paper’s texture.

A more discriminating question: **“Did rubbing the eraser abrade or roughen parts of the paper, creating the visible message through a difference in surface texture?”** This tests a physical mechanism not ruled out by the feedback; it does not assume the paper was punctured or torn.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did rubbing the eraser abrade or roughen parts of the paper, creating the visible message through a difference in surface texture?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A use the eraser to arrange eraser crumbs or shavings into the message on the paper?"}
review:
The crumbs hypothesis is plausible: it fits an immediately visible message without indenting, transferring marking substance, or roughening the paper. But the feedback doesn’t establish that eraser debris was involved, and “shavings” may imply material produced differently from ordinary crumbs.

A more discriminating question: **“Did A form the message from crumbs produced by rubbing the eraser on the paper?”**
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did A form the message from crumbs produced by rubbing the eraser on the paper?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A use the eraser as a tool or prop to make the message by a method that did not involve the eraser marking or changing the paper?"}
review:
The proposed question is too broad: “tool or prop” and “marking or changing the paper” bundle several possibilities, so either answer may be hard to interpret. The history already rules out many direct effects but does not establish that the eraser acted indirectly.

A more discriminating question: **“Was the eraser used to manipulate a separate object or material that then produced the message?”**
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did A use the eraser to manipulate a separate object or material that then produced the message on the paper?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A arrange separate objects on the paper so that their positions formed the message?"}
review:
This is a reasonable follow-up to the “separate object or material” **yes**, but it adds three unconfirmed details: multiple objects, placed on the paper, with their positions forming the message.

A more discriminating version is: **“Did A arrange multiple separate objects on the paper so that their placement itself spelled out the message?”** A “yes” would support the proposal; a “no” would leave open other ways the separate material produced the message.

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A use the eraser to operate or manipulate a writing instrument that then marked the paper?"}
review: The proposed question is plausible, but assumes the separate object was a writing instrument; the feedback only establishes that A manipulated a separate object or material. A broader, more discriminating question would be: **“Did the eraser physically actuate a mechanism that caused another object or material to produce the message?”** This tests the proposed mechanism without ruling out other possibilities prematurely.

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A use the eraser to hold or position another object that then made the message on the paper?"}
review:
The question is plausible, but “another object” is narrower than the earlier answer, which allowed a separate object **or material**. Also, “then made the message” leaves the method vague.

A clearer discriminator: **“Did A use the eraser to hold or position a separate material that directly produced the message on the paper?”** This tests the proposed idea without assuming a mechanism or excluding materials.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did A use the eraser to hold or position a separate material that directly produced the message on the paper?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A use the eraser to move a separate source of ink, pigment, or another marking substance across the paper so that it made the message?"}
review:
The proposed question is a reasonable branch to test: the history permits the eraser to manipulate a separate material, while ruling out several other ways of doing so. But it bundles two assumptions—that the material is a marking substance and that it is moved across the paper. A “no” would leave other ways for a separate material to produce the message unexplored.

A narrower question would be: **“Did the separate material A manipulated directly produce the visible message by depositing pigment or ink on the paper?”** This tests the marking-substance route without presuming how the material was moved.

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the separate material produce the message by changing the paper’s appearance through moisture or wetting it?"}
review:
The moisture question is a reasonable next test: the feedback leaves open a separate material creating the message without depositing ink or pigment. But “changing the paper’s appearance through moisture” is broad and may conflate wetting with the material’s identity.

A sharper question: **“Was the separate material a liquid, and did its contact with the paper itself make the message visible?”** This tests the moisture hypothesis without assuming the exact method.
